title: Flatiron Law Group's Lennie Nuara on Talent-First AI, M&A Workflows, and the Future of Legal Practice
author: Lennie Nuara

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI costs: Time savings obscure delivery economics
st.an: Nuara accepts that falling unit costs and expected efficiency gains do not establish better delivery economics. He materially develops the proposition by advocating clause- and run-level cost attribution and incorporating tool spending into transaction economics and fee quotes.
qs: Now, my experience has been at least the past two years, the token cost is going down, but the usage of how many agentic events that you have is going up.
And the cost of a tool is part of the economics of the transaction and how you quote.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Nuara aligns with continuous, cross-sector learning and materially extends it by linking awareness of frontier-model development to tool selection and the risk of model monoculture. His contribution is experiential and only loosely tied to research, however, and he does not directly address filtering quality or information overload.
qs: You gotta be looking to see where the models are.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: Nuara accepts the cluster’s expertise-pipeline concern and materially develops its adaptation agenda: foundational legal judgment should be built through hands-on, initially AI-independent training before trainees supervise AI. He also extends the concern beyond juniors to mid-career lawyers whose supervisory role may be disrupted, while proposing a paralegal-based talent pathway.
qs: The middle years, three to 10 or whatever it is now, the bigger firms, I think unless they adapt quickly,  are more challenged because a lot of what their work was doing was overseeing the various, you know, the years below them.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Nuara accepts the cluster’s emphasis on task-specific scrutiny and materially extends its apprenticeship response by proposing AI-driven simulation training for younger lawyers. His forecast that private equity will drive law-firm spending is speculative and does not establish institutional absorption or realised value.
qs: You have to be looking much more carefully at that.
Simulation training, that’s not just a plug for Deal Mentor, although it’s a great product, but we need more simulation training to create a more engaging environment for younger lawyers to learn.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: Nuara accepts selective, lawyer-supervised augmentation and materially develops it into a transaction-specific workflow: routine due-diligence and closing tasks can receive lighter verification, while consequential drafting requires richer source material and substantially deeper quality review. He offers practical examples rather than measured productivity evidence and does not address junior development or staffing leverage.
qs: And if you can extract the to and the from and the section of the agreement and so on and so forth, which then can be eyeballed by a partner or an associate, that they’re correct and they can go out, that’s great use of the tool.
And then you’re going to have to have a really serious analysis of the quality of it.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Nuara accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI should automate bounded production tasks under lawyer direction rather than replace lawyers. He materially extends it with a concrete, data-driven transaction-workflow model linking task decomposition and human-led AI to flat-fee pricing, while also identifying staffing, incentive and training implications. His claims are grounded mainly in firm experience rather than comparative measurement.
qs: There’s a core that doesn’t change, but in terms of the practice and the flow that what we’ve done is we did re-architect I like Paul re engineered the practice of the way we do deals and so from the very, very beginning ⁓ in our workflow we break things into smaller pieces.
We’re doing that now with AI and HI, but it’s it’s human driven.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Nuara accepts the cluster’s core proposition that legal AI requires selective, lawyer-led deployment rather than autonomous substitution. He materially extends it with a concrete operating model: decompose legal workflows into granular tasks, structure matter data, scale review to task risk, and place human verification checkpoints between agentic steps.
qs: There’s a core that doesn’t change, but in terms of the practice and the flow that what we’ve done is we did re-architect I like Paul re engineered the practice of the way we do deals and so from the very, very beginning ⁓ in our workflow we break things into smaller pieces.
The key, my perspective, is to stop and have HI, human intelligence, in between the steps.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Nuara supports the cluster’s central view that broader AI delegation makes human intervention and verification task-dependent. His transaction examples distinguish readily checked routine documents from higher-risk downstream drafting that requires substantially more rigorous quality review, while offering no measured evidence of broad autonomous reliability.
qs: But then as you go further downstream, you have a higher and higher risk value that you would place on a potential mistake or the misuse of the AI.

And if you can extract the to and the from and the section of the agreement and so on and so forth, which then can be eyeballed by a partner or an associate, that they’re correct and they can go out, that’s great use of the tool.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Nuara supports the cluster’s proposition that useful legal AI depends on task-specific workflows, sufficient context and retained lawyer checkpoints. His examples distinguish routine extraction, where supervised AI assistance is practical, from master-agreement drafting, where extensive source material and serious quality review are required.

And maybe you will, but you’re going to give it a lot of feedstock, a lot of documents that will essentially frame up what you’re looking for.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster by reporting rapid expansion in litigation AI while distinguishing product availability from demonstrated outcomes and promoting structured buyer evaluation. It supports the procurement-focused framing, but provides no evidence of adoption, workflow fit, realised value or improved case outcomes.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Nuara directly supports the cluster’s central paradox and response: AI may absorb formative junior work, so lawyers need substantial independent practice before relying on AI, supplemented by deliberate simulation training. His staffing and fee forecasts are qualified predictions rather than industry-wide evidence.
qs: Simulation training, that’s not just a plug for Deal Mentor, although it’s a great product, but we need more simulation training to create a more engaging environment for younger lawyers to learn.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Nuara supports the cluster’s account that AI pressures billable-hour economics and junior staffing while requiring lawyer-led oversight, substantial implementation effort and deliberate redesign of training. His flat-fee practice experience, proposed barbell staffing model and simulation-based apprenticeship response provide illustrative support, though they remain anecdotes and forecasts rather than market-wide evidence.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Nuara supports the cluster’s core framing of AI as lawyer-directed workflow redesign rather than wholesale lawyer substitution. He reinforces its emphasis on bounded delegation, substantive verification and experienced, client-specific judgment, but does not materially address the apprenticeship, funding or partner-succession proposals central to the expertise pipeline.

st.t: Legal data: Connected records enable operational transformation
st.an: The source supports the proposition that automation requires a sound data and workflow foundation rather than merely adding tools. Its document-extraction example also illustrates how structured data can create new operational visibility, though it provides anecdotal rather than quantified evidence and does not substantially address access governance or security.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: Nuara directly supports the cluster’s lawyer-guided framing: lawyers should direct AI, while transactional workflows are decomposed into suitable tasks for AI analysis. His account is experiential and does not establish autonomous delivery or quantified performance.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Nuara directly supports the proposition that legal AI’s benefits depend on organisational adaptation. kp.k: Lawyer talent should direct AI, not merely supervise it
kp.d: Nuara argues for a talent-first, AI-powered practice in which lawyers actively direct technology rather than merely remain in the loop. He treats AI as augmentation: deal strategy, negotiation, interpretation of counterparties and risk calibration remain counsel’s responsibilities. His account builds on Flatiron’s technology-enabled practice before generative AI rather than presenting AI as its starting point.
qs: It’s the practice of law is all about talent.
We’re not just in the loop. We should be driving it
using AI to support the lawyers

kp.k: Workflow redesign precedes and enables AI deployment
kp.d: Nuara describes reengineering transactions to avoid repeatedly reviewing the same documents during diligence, representations and warranties, closing and integration. Flatiron initially used remote workers and databases, incorporating workers costing $35–$50 an hour into flat fees; AI subsequently accelerated that architecture. These are practitioner reports of internal processes, not independently measured productivity findings.
qs: And they cost 35 to $50 an hour versus what it would have been within a firm for a client. And we just rolled that into our flat fee.
You’re going to go look for that same documents four times.
Now I’m doing it with AI and databases, but still databases

kp.k: Structured transaction data connects intake through closing
kp.d: Nuara says Flatiron starts with collecting and tracking diligence responses, not simply analyzing uploaded documents. Its platform links questions, responders, completion status and documents, then breaks documents into categories, clauses and sometimes phrases. Lawyers determine issues and extraction priorities; the resulting data supports reports, representations and warranties, assignment-consent analysis and closing checklists.
qs: We start even before that. We get the diligence on behalf of the clients by side, sell side.
The lawyers pick what they’re worried about.
There are areas, categories, subcategories, topics, the questions, the documents that relate to that stream.
You’re not at the word level, but you may be at the sentence or the phrase level, and now you have data points on all that.

kp.k: Diligence automation reduces repetitive work and staffing needs
kp.d: Nuara reports an average of 500 to 1,000 diligence questions per Flatiron deal and says the process now requires less human labor. He claims questions can have at least 10 and sometimes 30% overlap, making deduplication a useful AI application. AI intensity varies with document volume. His suggestion that displaced workers will move to other work is an expectation supported by manufacturing analogies, not employment evidence.
qs: But on average for us, it’s 500 to 1,000 diligence questions per deal.
We don’t need as much of that anymore.
In the 500 to 1000 questions, I guarantee you there’s like at least 10 and sometimes a 30 % overlap.
Some of the early class might be displaced, but ultimately they’ll be pushed off to do other things and other things well.

kp.k: AI review should reflect task-specific legal risk
kp.d: Nuara distinguishes relatively low-risk deduplication from higher-risk drafting, playbook review and master agreements. Standard closing letters can be populated from extracted data and checked by a partner or associate; substantial agreements require more source material and serious quality analysis. He warns from experience that fluent drafts can omit necessary issues or reverse intended provisions. He offers no universal threshold for sufficient review, locating that decision in experienced human judgment.
qs: If you’re drafting documents, it’s another use of AI. Much higher risk profile than finding duplicates, right?
which then can be eyeballed by a partner or an associate, that they’re correct and they can go out
And then you’re going to have to have a really serious analysis of the quality of it.
I can’t give you a quantum. That’s a quality issue that the H.I., the human intelligence factor, is critical on.

kp.k: Agentic workflows require human verification between steps
kp.d: Nuara recommends small, inspectable tasks for both AI and junior lawyers, arguing that decomposition improves reliability and makes errors easier to locate. He supports agentic components but rejects unchecked chains of agents, recommending human verification between stages. His reliability claims are practice-based judgments rather than benchmark results.
qs: The higher likelihood of success that you will have with it, the bigger task that you give it, the worse it will be.
The key, my perspective, is to stop and have HI, human intelligence, in between the steps.
Many people are building agentic workflows. Great, OK, but there’s no verification opportunity between the agents.
You can trust them to do something, but if you do it in small pieces, you’ll find the mistake in that one place.

kp.k: Senior process-design investment conflicts with existing firm incentives
kp.d: Nuara argues that experienced practitioners must invest substantial time in decomposing workflows before technology can deliver later efficiencies; operational staff alone cannot supply their expertise. He attributes his flexibility to Flatiron’s lack of a traditional labor stack and contrasts his investment with a firm’s reported allowance of 50 or 100 annual associate innovation hours. He says large firms may need to change roles, performance expectations and compensation to enable comparable investment.
qs: They’re not efficient, but hopefully it will be a multiplier for later when they invest the time now.
I could spend an extra 200 hours in a month.
Firms need to look at that and they can do that with their ops group, but at some point the real talent needs to spend that time.

kp.k: Iterative elicitation makes tacit legal workflows explicit
kp.d: Nuara recommends having lawyers repeatedly dictate or describe a deal’s sequence, using AI to expand it into a task list, then having lawyers identify omissions. He regards this as a relatively low-risk use that leverages lawyers’ ability to critique written material, while emphasizing that decisions about automating particular legal tasks still vary with their risks.
qs: Okay, now put that into AI and say, write out this process and show me the steps in the process.
Lawyers are really good at finding a problem with your stuff.
not telling you in advance what the problem will be, but reacting to something on paper.

kp.k: Conformist drafting threatens deal-specific professional judgment
kp.d: Nuara argues that convergence toward common language is a greater drafting risk than hallucinations because standard provisions may fail to advance a particular client’s negotiating position. He attributes this to overlapping training sources, including SEC EDGAR contracts, and limited private-transaction data. These are his assertions; his references to Stanford research do not identify a study or result. His expectation that hallucinations will improve over time is a prediction, not an established finding.
qs: That will ultimately clean up over time. It’s conformity.
So you’ll get what everyone else did. That’s not what you need in your deal.
Example, they’re all looking at the Edgar database from the SEC for contract clauses.
Very troublesome, there’s not a lot of data on the private transaction.
Get me the best deal you can get based upon my circumstances. Don’t get me what’s standard.

kp.k: Precedents and multiple models still produce first drafts
kp.d: Nuara says Flatiron supplies prior deals that push drafting in a desired direction and can compare several models through its platform, but he currently sees broadly similar performance and treats outputs as first passes. He is skeptical of generic playbooks for Flatiron’s varied deals, while acknowledging their potential usefulness for a recurring enterprise client. He suggests larger firms might exploit their larger precedent collections through retrieval-augmented drafting.
qs: if I was representing the same client all the time, always I might I might revert to that
We pull our old deals and we put them in and it’ll create a first pass, but it is still literally just still a first pass.
the mega firms, the big law, they have a corpus that they can point to that are significantly larger than what we have.

kp.d: Nuara says Flatiron currently has no associates but is developing a staffing model combining substantial senior talent with very junior lawyers and capable non-lawyers, leaving a thinner middle. He describes potential recruitment of people unwilling to spend $100,000 or $200,000 on law school. He predicts particular challenges for lawyers in years three to ten whose work has included supervising juniors. This is a proposed structure and forecast, not an implemented firm-wide staffing outcome.

You’ll have a ton of senior talent here. You have a ton of very young lawyers here and in the middle you may have a thinner path.

kp.k: Formation requires unaided practice alongside AI simulation
kp.d: Nuara recommends that early-career workers first perform substantive work without AI to develop issue-spotting knowledge they can later use to oversee it. He also advocates more engaging AI-generated negotiation simulations, citing Deal Mentor and his work with Megan Ma. He warns that otherwise training may skip years of development; he presents no comparative evidence of simulation effectiveness.
qs: And they spend time not on AI to do those things.

kp.k: Flat fees expose hourly compensation and staffing tensions
kp.d: Nuara says Flatiron accepts the economic risk of flat fees and redesigns workflows to quote them more efficiently. He argues that large firms resist because efficiency threatens recorded hours, utilization of existing staff and individual compensation, even when a deal is completed successfully. He expects this tension to encourage alternative fee structures but stresses the difficulty of changing established firms.

you don’t have the thousand hours, so what you but you finish the deal
Am I going to get compensated? That should drive them towards a different fee structure.

kp.k: Granular AI cost accounting supports transaction pricing
kp.d: Nuara reports that Deal Driver tracks AI costs by clause, model and agentic run, aggregating them to documents and broader document collections. He says token prices have fallen in his experience over the past two years while agentic usage has risen, making visibility important for quotes and accountability. His expectation of enormous efficiency gains, expressed as approximately a hundred to one, is a belief rather than a demonstrated cost study.
qs: you can see that you’ve ran 14 different agentic flows and what the cost of each run is for the clause in that one document.
the cost of a tool is part of the economics of the transaction and how you quote.
the token cost is going down, but the usage of how many agentic events that you have is going up.
It’s like, you know, a hundred to one, but it’s still, you have to recognize that that’s a cost and many vendors do not expose that.

kp.k: Buyer pressure may accelerate pricing and organizational change
kp.d: Nuara predicts that private-equity buyers will press harder than other enterprises to reduce legal spending as they recognize AI’s capabilities. He expects pressure on large firms’ billing capacity, possible movement toward flat fees and changes to pyramid staffing. His private-equity argument concerns pressure on legal expenditure, not a claim about non-lawyer ownership or regulatory reform.
qs: They’ll push harder than the enterprises will, although enterprises will push, but private equity will push even harder.
that will drive a spend cycle that’s going to compress the big firm ability to bill.
And then maybe they’ll switch to flat fees or otherwise.
AI is going to absorb a lot of junior level work.

kp.k: New legal demand could moderate labor displacement
kp.d: Nuara qualifies his displacement forecast by recalling growth in regulatory practice and transaction complexity since he began practicing in 1984. He suggests new work could similarly offset some effects of efficiency and recommends retraining and redeploying lawyers rather than assuming firms will collapse. The regulatory comparison is a historical practitioner analogy, not a quantified forecast of future employment.
qs: The only other thing that might happen that will ameliorate that is just the nature of the practice of law.
the regulatory practices has exploded as a percentage of what a law firm does and the complexity on every transaction around the regulatory sector.
I don’t think they’re going to break, but what people do and how they do it is definitely going to change.
the smart firms will figure out how to repurpose people in different ways

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Lennie Nuara describes AI as a lawyer-directed tool that reduces transactional processing work, while predicting changes to staffing, training, pricing and competitive pressures rather than the disappearance of legal judgment.
pts.d: Nuara's claims span several areas. (1) Talent-first practice: lawyers should direct AI, not merely remain in the loop; strategy, negotiation, risk calibration and client-specific judgment remain human responsibilities. (2) Transactional workflows: Flatiron decomposes diligence into structured questions, documents, clauses and data points, then reuses those data downstream for reports, representations and warranties, and closing documents. AI now performs extraction previously undertaken by people and reduces the human capacity required. He also describes AI deduplication of overlapping diligence requests. These changes extend a workflow redesign that began before generative AI. (3) Reliability: smaller tasks and human verification between agentic steps increase the likelihood of useful results; polished drafting can omit substantive requirements or reverse intended outcomes. (4) Drafting conformity: Nuara argues that models drawing on overlapping sources converge toward standard provisions rather than the client's best negotiating position. He regards this as a greater drafting risk than hallucinations and predicts hallucinations will improve over time. Targeted instructions and relevant precedents can improve drafts, but they remain first passes. (5) Economics: he expects AI to be substantially more efficient than people for assigned tasks, illustratively invoking a hundred-to-one factor, while insisting that token and agentic execution costs must be tracked. (6) Staffing and training: AI will absorb substantial junior-level work; he proposes a barbell structure with substantial senior and very junior capacity and a thinner middle. Junior lawyers and capable nonlawyers need foundational work without dependence on AI, complemented by AI-driven simulation training. (7) Market pressure: private-equity clients will press legal providers harder on spending than enterprise clients generally, compressing large firms' ability to bill and potentially encouraging flat fees. Firms will need to redeploy and retrain people, with growing legal complexity potentially creating offsetting work.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Nuara primarily offers practitioner experience, descriptions of his own systems and illustrative quantities; the broader predictions are not presented as measured industry findings.
pts.d: Nuara grounds the workflow claims in Flatiron's flat-fee transactional practice and his earlier use of remote workers and databases for extracting and reusing document data. He reports 500–1,000 diligence questions per deal and approximately 10–30% overlap among questions, without providing a dataset, measurement method or independent assessment. He draws on experience reviewing convincing but incomplete AI drafts, comparing models and supplying prior deal documents. For cost claims, he describes Deal Driver's tracking by clause, model, agentic run, document and aggregate usage, and reports falling token prices alongside rising agentic activity over the preceding two years. The hundred-to-one efficiency comparison is his illustrative expectation, not a documented benchmark or a demonstrated end-to-end saving inclusive of verification. His staffing proposal is partly a model developed on paper, informed by earlier nonlawyer staffing experience; he explicitly says the firm currently has no associates. He cites unspecified reading about overlapping training corpora and unspecified Stanford research when discussing model conformity, without identifying a particular study or reporting a result that can be attributed to a named benchmark or to the Stanford RegLab hallucination study. Deal Mentor supplies a concrete example of AI-generated negotiation simulation, but no comparative learning outcomes are supplied. Predictions about private-equity pressure, billing compression, workforce restructuring and eventual hallucination improvement are professional forecasts. Historical growth in regulatory practice is offered as an analogy for how new work might offset automation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current operational claims are conditional on task design, volume, risk and expert oversight; broader forecasts have no fixed delivery date.
pts.d: In the transcript labeled 2026, Nuara describes current Flatiron workflows as an extension of systems begun more than nine years earlier, before generative AI. His anecdote about misleadingly polished drafts refers to approximately two years earlier, and his token-cost observation covers the past two years. AI use scales with document volume: smaller matters may need little AI. Dedupe and routine closing-letter tasks carry different risks from master-agreement drafting, indemnification and transaction-specific risk allocation. Higher-risk work requires more contextual material and serious lawyer review. He offers no quantitative stopping rule for verification, instead locating that decision in experience and judgment. Agentic workflows should include human verification between steps. Building them requires an initial efficiency sacrifice by senior practitioners, with hoped-for later returns; large firms may need to change roles, targets and compensation to permit that investment. His skepticism about playbooks is qualified by Flatiron's varied clients and bespoke deals: repeated representation of one client could justify their use. Larger firms' private precedent collections might improve drafting through retrieval, but this is a possibility rather than a demonstrated outcome. Staffing changes depend on adaptation, foundational training and the ability to repurpose people. The closing forecasts respond to a near-term future question but provide no calendar deadline. Flat-fee adoption is expressly tentative, and expanded legal or regulatory work may ameliorate displacement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are transactional clients, junior and middle-career legal workers, senior lawyers, and law firms facing new delivery economics and client spending pressure.
pts.d: For M&A buyers and sellers, Nuara describes reduced duplication in diligence, better tracking and reuse of information, and more efficient production of transaction materials. Their interests can nevertheless be poorly served if standard AI drafting substitutes for client-specific negotiation judgment. Routine extraction workers and junior lawyers face reduced demand for some existing tasks; very junior lawyers and capable nonlawyers may also enter redesigned training and delivery structures. He identifies lawyers approximately three to ten years into practice at larger firms as particularly challenged unless they adapt, because some of their work involves supervising more junior staff. Senior lawyers retain responsibility for strategy, risk and verification, but must invest substantial time in documenting and redesigning workflows. Flatiron's lean structure and flat-fee model provide flexibility for this investment; larger firms face compensation, billing-target and staffing constraints, although their larger precedent collections may offer an advantage in contextualizing AI drafts. Private-equity clients are forecast to intensify spending pressure on outside counsel, with other enterprise clients also exerting pressure. AI simulations are presented as a way to make younger lawyers' learning more engaging and avoid leaving a developmental gap. Nuara suggests the workflow principles can extend beyond M&A to other transactional, litigation and regulatory practices. These are principally commercial legal-service claims, not claims about closing the civil access-to-justice gap.
